questions.prompt: Which mental model best explains “CSS Runtime Performance” in Dart Sass?
options: The best solution is always to replace native CSS behavior with a new Sass abstraction.
Measure the part of the pipeline you want to improve. Sass affects build-time work and the CSS it emits; the browser still performs style calculation, layout, and rendering using that output.
The browser executes Sass source directly, so a compilation step is unnecessary.
Readable SCSS guarantees correct browser rendering, accessibility, and performance without output review.
questions.answer_key: Measure the part of the pipeline you want to improve. Sass affects build-time work and the CSS it emits; the browser still performs style calculation, layout, and rendering using that output.
questions.explanation: Measure the part of the pipeline you want to improve. Sass affects build-time work and the CSS it emits; the browser still performs style calculation, layout, and rendering using that output. The alternative choices confuse Sass compilation with browser execution or claim guarantees that require independent tests.

questions.prompt: When applying “Understanding the difference between compilation and browser rendering”, which approach is the most reliable?
options: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact.
Skip compilation and infer the final selector list and property values from the source file alone.
Prefer deeply nested selectors because fewer source lines always mean simpler and safer CSS.
Silence every warning before determining whether it identifies a deprecated or incorrect construct.
questions.answer_key: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact.
questions.explanation: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact. Compare the compiled output with the stated intent and preserve browser-native behavior where it is required.

questions.prompt: Which review decision most directly supports maintainability for “CSS Runtime Performance”?
options: Generate every possible selector or theme combination, even when most variants are never used.
Treat successful compilation as proof that the interface is accessible and behaves correctly in every browser.
Expose internal implementation details as public API and postpone documentation until after release.

Prefer a small, explicit output over a clever generator with many combinations. Compare CSS size and representative browser behavior before and after changes instead of treating compact source as a performance metric.
questions.answer_key: Prefer a small, explicit output over a clever generator with many combinations. Compare CSS size and representative browser behavior before and after changes instead of treating compact source as a performance metric.
questions.explanation: Prefer a small, explicit output over a clever generator with many combinations. Compare CSS size and representative browser behavior before and after changes instead of treating compact source as a performance metric. The other choices increase output, assume unverified behavior, or make the public interface harder to maintain.
